If the derivative is a total return swap or similar structure where the underlying asset's maturity dictates the funding obligation, the initial or residual maturity of the underlying asset should be used. However, for standard interest rate or currency swaps where the obligation is fixed until the contract's end, the initial maturity of the derivative contract itself is the appropriate metric.

In cases where the specific maturity cannot be clearly defined or if the liability is effectively demandable, a conservative approach of assuming a one-day maturity may be applied to ensure the LCR is not overstated. This aligns with the principle of prudence in liquidity risk management. The EBA's technical standards and guidance emphasize that the maturity used must reflect the earliest date on which the institution could reasonably be expected to be required to repay the liability or deliver the collateral. Therefore, for fair value of derivatives and non-standard collaterals, the initial maturity of the derivative contract or the underlying asset, whichever is shorter and most restrictive, should be reported to maintain the integrity of the liquidity buffers.

question: For exiting the non-performing category Art. 17 no. 157 requires that one year has passed since the forbearance measures were extended. Does that mean that, a) the probation period starts already at the date of the forbearance measure. b) The probation period starts only when the exposure is no longer considered impaired or defaulted.
ground_truth: For the purposes of Art. 17 par. 157 (b) of the draft ITS on Supervisory reporting regarding exit criteria of non-performing exposures with forbearance measures, the one year cure period starts running since the date when the forbearance measures were extended. For the sake of completeness, it should be pointed out that according to Art. 17 par. 176, a minimum 2 year probation period starting as soon as the exposure is considered as "performing", is required in order to exit from the forborne category. Therefore non performing forborne exposures shall stay in the forborne exposure category for at least 3 years (1 year at least in the non-performing forborne exposure category for the cure period stated by Art. 17 par. 157 (b) and 2 years at least in the performing forborne exposure category for the probation period required by Art. 17 par. 176).

meta.subject_matter: Start of Probation Period

baseline.text: Under Article 17(157) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the requirement for an exposure to remain in the non-performing category for one year is strictly tied to the date of the *extension* of forbearance measures, not the initial classification or the subsequent removal of impairment. Consequently, the probation period commences on the specific date the forbearance measure is extended, as this date marks the new reference point for the one-year duration mandated by the regulation [CRR, Art. 17(157)]. The legislative intent is to ensure that exposures subject to extended forbearance are monitored for a full year of non-performance before they can be reclassified as performing, regardless of whether the exposure was previously impaired or defaulted. Therefore, option (a) is correct: the probation period starts at the date the forbearance measure is extended. Option (b) is incorrect because the start of the probation period is an administrative trigger based on the extension event, not a conditional event dependent on the credit quality of the exposure. If an exposure is reclassified as performing prior to the expiration of this one-year period following an extension, it does not retroactively invalidate the probation period; rather, the exposure remains classified as non-performing until the full year has elapsed from the extension date. This interpretation aligns with the technical standards issued by the European Banking Authority (EBA) regarding the implementation of the CRR, which clarify that the "one year" condition is a temporal constraint linked to the forbearance timeline rather than a credit assessment outcome [EBA, Technical Standards on Supervisory Reporting of Non-Performing Exposures]. The regulatory framework ensures consistency in supervisory reporting by anchoring the probation period to the specific act of extending forbearance, thereby preventing premature reclassification that could undermine the stability of the non-performing exposure statistics.

dpo.text: Under Article 17(157) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the requirement for a one-year probation period applies specifically to exposures that have been reclassified as non-performing following the extension of forbearance measures. The regulation stipulates that an exposure shall be considered non-performing only if it has been in that category for at least one year since the forbearance measures were extended [CRR, Art. 17(157)]. This temporal condition is a prerequisite for the classification itself, not merely a condition for exiting the category. Consequently, the "probation period" in this context refers to the duration during which the exposure remains classified as non-performing while the one-year clock runs. Therefore, the probation period commences at the date the forbearance measures are extended, not when the exposure is subsequently reclassified as performing. If the exposure were to be reclassified as performing before the one-year period elapsed, the regulatory condition for maintaining the non-performing status would not be met, and the exposure would no longer be subject to the specific reporting requirements associated with that classification. The logic of the provision is to ensure that institutions maintain a conservative stance on exposures under forbearance for a minimum duration, regardless of interim credit quality assessments, until the full year has passed since the extension. Thus, option (a) is correct: the probation period starts at the date of the forbearance measure extension. Option (b) is incorrect because the start of the period is tied to the extension event, not the outcome of the credit review. This interpretation aligns with the EBA's technical standards on supervisory reporting, which clarify that the one-year threshold is a fixed temporal marker for the extension date to determine eligibility for the non-performing classification [EBA-GL-2016-01, Section 4.2].

question:
Consider a corporate (geographical location DE) exposure guaranteed by a sovereign (geographical location NL).
1) Do the CRM techniques with substitution effect (e.g. guarantees) impact the scoping of relevant exposures for the purposes of the Countercyclical Buffer? E.g. should a corporate exposure with a sovereign guarantee be considered a relevant exposure as sovereign exposures are not considered relevant in accordance with Article 140 of the Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD).
2) If the exposure is considered relevant, should CRM techniques with substitution effects be taken into account for the purposes of the calculation of the capital requirements for the purposes of the determination of the weighted average referred to in Article 140(1) CRD? E.g. can a sovereign guarantee be taken into account in the calculation of the capital requirement for a corporate exposure with a sovereign guarantee?
3) Article 84 of the (draft) ITS 2014/680 Annex 2 (as revised on 8 March 2016) requires geographical allocation on immediate obligor basis, i.e. any CRM (e.g. cross-border guarantee) should not change the geographical location to the location of the CRM provider. The BCBS FAQ on the Basel III Countercyclical Capital Buffer requires the usage of ‘jurisdiction of ultimate risk’, which substitutes the exposure to the location of the CRM provider. Can you please clarify which geographical location should be used for calculation and reporting of the CCyB and template C09.04?
ground_truth:
According to Article 1(4) of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 1152/2014 (RTS on geographical location), in order to determine the geographical location, the exposures are allocated on an immediate obligor basis. Therefore CRM techniques do not change the allocation of an exposure to its geographical location for the purpose of calculation of countercyclical capital buffer.
In this regard:
1)     A corporate exposure is a relevant exposure in accordance with Article 140(4)(a) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD), even if it is partially or fully secured by an eligible guarantee by a government, as the immediate source of risk is not to the sovereign.
2)     The calculation of the capital requirements is based on all applicable provisions of Part Three, Title II of CRR, including those on credit risk mitigation. While the assignment to a country depends solely on the location of the immediate obligor as defined in the RTS on the geographical location, the own funds requirement is calculated taking into account eligible sovereign guarantees and other credit risk mitigants.
3)     For the purposes of reporting template C 09.04 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory Reporting), and as defined in Part II, paragraph
85
84
of the ITS on Supervisory Reporting, the geographical location of of the immediate obligor shall be used.

meta.subject_matter: Calculation of the Countercyclical Capital Buffer

baseline.text:
Regarding the impact of Credit Risk Mitigation (CRM) techniques with a substitution effect on the scoping of relevant exposures for the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), the treatment depends on the specific nature of the guarantee. Under Article 140 of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD), sovereign exposures are explicitly excluded from the definition of relevant exposures. However, this exclusion does not automatically apply to corporate exposures that are fully guaranteed by a sovereign. According to the EBA's Technical Standards (ITS) 2014/680 Annex 2, a corporate exposure remains a relevant exposure even if it is fully guaranteed by a sovereign, provided the guarantee does not eliminate the credit risk associated with the corporate obligor. Consequently, such exposures must be included in the CCyB calculation, as the substitution effect does not transform the underlying corporate risk into a sovereign risk for scoping purposes [ITS 2014/680, Annex 2, Section 1.1].

For the second issue, if the exposure is deemed relevant, CRM techniques with a substitution effect must be taken into account when calculating the capital requirements for the determination of the weighted average referred to in Article 140(1) CRD. Specifically, the credit risk mitigation provided by the sovereign guarantee can be used to reduce the exposure amount subject to the CCyB charge, provided the guarantee meets the eligibility criteria set out in the ITS. This allows institutions to utilize the sovereign guarantee to lower the capital requirement, effectively mitigating the risk weight applied to the corporate exposure [ITS 2014/680, Annex 2, Section 1.2].

Regarding the geographical allocation for calculation and reporting, Article 84 of the ITS 2014/680 Annex 2 mandates that geographical allocation be performed on the basis of the immediate obligor's location. This means that for a corporate exposure guaranteed by a sovereign, the geographical location remains that of the corporate obligor (in this case, Germany), regardless of the location of the guarantee provider (Netherlands). The Basel Committee's FAQ on the 'jurisdiction of ultimate risk' does not override this specific requirement for the CCyB under EU law. Therefore, for the purpose of calculating and reporting the CCyB and in template C09.04, the geographical location must be assigned to the immediate obligor (Germany), ensuring consistency with the EU regulatory framework which prioritizes the location of the primary borrower over the location of the mitigating instrument [ITS 2014/680, Annex 2, Section 1.3].

dpo.text:
Regarding the impact of Credit Risk Mitigation (CRM) techniques with a substitution effect on the scoping of relevant exposures for the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), Article 140(1) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) establishes that relevant exposures are those where the counterparty is located in the Union and the exposure is not covered by a guarantee from a third country. Consequently, a corporate exposure guaranteed by a Dutch sovereign is not considered a relevant exposure for CCyB purposes because the guarantee originates from a third country, effectively removing the exposure from the scope of Article 140 [CRD, Article 140(1)].

If the exposure were deemed relevant, Article 140(1) further stipulates that CRM techniques with a substitution effect must be taken into account when calculating the capital requirements. This means that if a corporate exposure with a sovereign guarantee were relevant, the guarantee would reduce the exposure amount used for the calculation of the weighted average referred to in Article 140(1) [CRD, Article 140(1)]. However, since the exposure is excluded from the scope due to the third-country guarantee, this calculation step is not triggered.

Concerning the geographical allocation for CCyB calculation and reporting under Template C09.04, Article 84 of the draft ITS 2014/680 Annex 2 (as revised on 8 March 2016) mandates allocation on the immediate obligor basis. This rule explicitly requires that CRM techniques, including cross-border guarantees, do not alter the geographical location of the exposure to the location of the CRM provider. Therefore, the corporate exposure remains allocated to Germany, the location of the immediate obligor, rather than shifting to the Netherlands, the location of the guarantor. This approach aligns with the EBA's technical standards which prioritize the immediate obligor's jurisdiction over the 'jurisdiction of ultimate risk' concept found in the BCBS FAQ, ensuring consistency in the reporting template [ITS 2014/680, Annex 2, Article 84].

question:
How to apply the even deduction rule stipulated in the Article 5(2) of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63 and further clarified by the EBA Q&A
2015_1893
(Treatment of specific liabilities - even deduction) in cases where each party books the transaction in different amount?
ground_truth:
In case of mismatch between entity A and B, the value booked as a liability should prevail, because the exclusion under Article 5(1)(a) Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63 (DR on ex ante contributions to resolution financing arrangements) concerns intragroup liabilities.
Disclaimer:
This question goes beyond matters of consistent and effective application of the regulatory framework. A Directorate General of the Commission (Directorate General Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union) has prepared the answer, albeit that only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide definitive interpretations of EU legislation. This is an unofficial opinion of that Directorate General, which the European Banking Authority publishes on its behalf. The answers are not binding on the European Commission as an institution. You should be aware that the European Commission could adopt a position different from the one expressed in such Q&As, for instance in infringement proceedings or after a detailed examination of a specific case or on the basis of any new legal or factual elements that may have been brought to its attention.

meta.subject_matter: Application of the even deduction rule in case of intragroup transactions booked - by institutions which are parties to the contract - in different amounts

baseline.text:
The application of the even deduction rule under Article 5(2) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63, as clarified in EBA Q&A 2015_1893, requires a strict adherence to the principle that the deduction must be identical for both the creditor and the debtor within the same resolution scenario, regardless of the initial book values recorded by each institution. When intragroup transactions are booked in different amounts due to distinct accounting policies, fair value adjustments, or intercompany profit elimination, the resolution authority must not utilize the disparate book values to determine the deduction amount. Instead, the rule mandates that the deduction be calculated based on the amount that would have been recorded if the transaction had been settled at fair value at the time of the resolution, ensuring symmetry in the treatment of specific liabilities.

Consequently, if Institution A books a receivable at €100 million while Institution B books the corresponding payable at €80 million, the deduction applied to both entities must be the same figure, typically derived from the fair value of the underlying asset or liability at the resolution date. The EBA guidance explicitly states that the difference in book values does not justify a differential deduction; rather, the resolution framework aims to prevent artificial capital erosion or artificial capital preservation that could arise from inconsistent accounting treatments. The resolution authority is tasked with determining a single, consistent deduction amount that reflects the economic reality of the transaction at the point of resolution, effectively neutralizing the impact of prior accounting discrepancies. This ensures that the resolution process treats the intragroup relationship as a single economic unit, preventing one institution from retaining more capital than the other solely due to accounting mechanics rather than actual risk exposure. The final deduction figure must be applied uniformly to both parties to maintain the integrity of the resolution plan and the stability of the financial system.

[Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63, Article 5(2)]
[EBA Q&A 2015_1893, Paragraph 12]

dpo.text:
The application of the even deduction rule under Article 5(2) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/63, as clarified in EBA Q&A 2015_1893, requires a strict adherence to the principle that the deduction must be identical for both the creditor and the debtor within the same resolution scenario, regardless of the initial book values recorded by each institution. When intragroup transactions are booked in different amounts due to distinct accounting policies, fair value adjustments, or intercompany profit elimination methods, the resolution authority must not simply mirror the debtor's recorded liability against the creditor's asset. Instead, the authority must determine a single, consistent deduction amount that reflects the economic substance of the transaction at the time of resolution. This ensures that the resolution process does not artificially inflate or deflate the capital requirements of the group entities based on accounting discrepancies rather than economic reality.

Specifically, the EBA guidance mandates that if the creditor has recognized a higher asset value than the debtor has recognized a corresponding liability reduction, the deduction applied to the creditor's asset must be adjusted downward to match the deduction applied to the debtor's liability. Conversely, if the debtor's liability is recorded at a lower amount, the creditor's asset deduction must be increased to maintain parity. The core objective is to prevent the creation of artificial capital buffers or deficits that would distort the resolution plan's viability. The resolution authority is tasked with identifying the "true" economic exposure and applying this uniform deduction across the group. This approach aligns with the broader BRRD framework aimed at ensuring the stability of the financial system during resolution, preventing the erosion of common equity through inconsistent accounting treatments. Consequently, institutions must provide robust evidence to the resolution authority demonstrating how the even deduction was calculated, ensuring transparency and consistency in the treatment of specific liabilities across the entire resolution group.

question: According to Fin-FSA and based on national regulation (Sijoituspalvelulaki 747/2012) the capital conservation buffer should not be applied to investment firms with personnel under 250 and balance sheet amount under 43 million. Validation rule v8714_m requires that this row (CA4_r750) is reported. How should the capital conservation buffer be reported in this case?
ground_truth:
According to article 129 (2) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD), a Member State may exempt small and medium-sized investment firms from the requirements set out in that paragraph if such an exemption does not threaten the stability of the financial system of that Member State.
As notified by the FIN-FSA (Finland national competent authority) to EBA, this exemption has been exercised via the Act on Investment Firms 747/2012, and therefore, VR v8714_m shall not apply to Finnish investment firms classified as SMEs following article 129 (4) of CRD.
VR v8714_m has a “warning” type of severity and will therefore remain as such to allow for the cases described in this Q&A.

meta.subject_matter: National regulation contradicts with Directive 2013/36 - v8714

baseline.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the capital conservation buffer is a mandatory requirement applicable to all credit institutions and investment firms meeting the definition in Article 4(1)(1) and (2) of Directive 2013/36/EU, regardless of their size or number of employees. The threshold exemptions for the capital conservation buffer do not exist within the CRR framework itself; the buffer applies uniformly to all entities subject to the prudential requirements of the regulation. Consequently, the national regulation cited, Sijoituspalvelulaki 747/2012, which attempts to exclude investment firms with fewer than 250 employees or a balance sheet below 43 million euros from the capital conservation buffer, is inconsistent with the mandatory scope of CRR Article 450(1).

In the context of COREP reporting, specifically row CA4_r750, the validation rule v8714_m correctly enforces the requirement that this data point must be reported for all eligible entities. The reporting obligation is distinct from the calculation of the buffer amount. Even if a national authority were to apply a specific exemption (which would be legally impermissible under EU law), the entity remains obligated to report the buffer level. If the entity is deemed to have a zero buffer due to the non-application of the requirement, the value reported in CA4_r750 must be 0.00. However, the entity cannot simply omit the row or report it as "not applicable." The validation rule ensures data completeness, and the reporting entity must reflect the regulatory reality that the buffer is either calculated and reported or, in the case of a zero buffer, reported as zero. Any national provision contradicting the mandatory application of the capital conservation buffer to investment firms under CRR is invalid and must be disregarded for the purpose of supervisory reporting. Therefore, the entity must report the calculated buffer amount, which will be zero if the entity falls below the minimum capital requirements but is still subject to the buffer regime, or the specific buffer amount if applicable, ensuring full compliance with CRR Article 450.

dpo.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the capital conservation buffer is a mandatory requirement applicable to all credit institutions and investment firms meeting the definition in Article 4(1)(1) and (2) of Directive 2013/36/EU, respectively, without exception based on size or personnel thresholds. The exemption for smaller entities applies only to the *additional* capital requirements under Article 92(1) of CRR, not to the buffer itself. Consequently, the validation rule v8714_m, which mandates the reporting of row CA4_r750 (Capital conservation buffer) for all reporting entities, correctly reflects the legal obligation to disclose the buffer amount, even if the calculated value is zero.

The requirement to report the buffer is derived from the supervisory reporting framework established in CRR Article 100(1), which mandates the submission of data on capital requirements and buffers. Specifically, CRR Article 100(1)(a) requires the reporting of the "capital conservation buffer" as a distinct line item. The absence of a buffer due to the entity's size does not negate the reporting obligation; rather, it results in a reported value of zero. Therefore, Fin-FSA's interpretation that the buffer should not be applied is legally incorrect regarding the *application* of the buffer to the calculation, but the *reporting* of the result (zero) remains mandatory.

Directive 2013/36/EU, as amended by Directive (EU) 2019/379, defines the scope of investment firms subject to capital requirements in Article 4(1)(2). This definition is inclusive and does not contain the size-based exclusions found in the prudential capital requirements of CRR Article 92. Thus, an investment firm with fewer than 250 employees and a balance sheet below €43 million remains subject to the capital conservation buffer regime under CRR Article 92(2). The validation rule v8714_m ensures transparency by requiring the disclosure of the buffer level, which must be reported as zero if the entity is not subject to the buffer requirement under specific national derogations or if the calculation yields zero, but the row itself must be populated. National regulations cannot override the explicit reporting mandates of the CRR.

[Source, Article/Paragraph] CRR Article 100(1)(a); CRR Article 92(2); Directive 2013/36/EU Article 4(1)(2); Directive (EU) 2019/379 Article 1(1).

meta.subject_matter: Annex VI, template C 108.00, Definition of P&L

baseline.text: Under Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD), the definition of P&L for template C 108.00 in Annex VI refers specifically to the actual P&L, adjusted for Theta, settled cash flows, and other relevant factors, rather than the P&L Vector derived from historical market simulations. The regulatory framework distinguishes clearly between the statistical inputs used for risk measurement and the realized financial performance reported to supervisors. Template C 108.00 is designed to capture the institution's actual economic outcome over the reporting period, ensuring that supervisory assessments reflect real-world performance rather than hypothetical scenarios. While the P&L Vector generated using historically simulated daily market price or risk factor movements serves as a critical input for calculating Value at Risk (VaR) and other risk metrics, it represents a probabilistic distribution of potential losses, not the realized profit or loss. Consequently, the definition mandated for C 108.00 excludes these simulated figures. The requirement to adjust the actual P&L for Theta accounts for the time decay of options and derivatives, while settled cash flows ensure that the reported figure reflects the net economic position after all transactions have been finalized. This distinction is fundamental to the integrity of the supervisory reporting process, as it allows regulators to evaluate the institution's true risk exposure and capital adequacy based on factual data. The EBA's technical standards and guidelines consistently emphasize that supervisory reporting templates must provide a clear, unambiguous picture of the institution's financial standing, which is best achieved through the reporting of actual, adjusted P&L figures. Therefore, institutions must ensure that the data submitted for C 108.00 aligns with the actual economic results, meticulously adjusted for time value and cash settlements, to comply with the reporting obligations set forth in the directive.

question: Can a person that is not authorised as an investment firm but meets the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II be a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF?
ground_truth:
[ESMA 70-872942901-38 MiFID II MiFIR market structures Q&A, Q&A 5.4]
Yes. Article 53(3) of MiFID II provides that an entity that is not an investment firm or a credit institution can be a member of a regulated market under certain conditions, this rule being extended to MTFs by Article 19(2) of MiFID II.
ESMA considers that this provision should be read in conjunction with the requirements of Article 2(1). Under this provision, a person falling under any of the categories listed in Article 2(1) would not have to be authorised as an investment firm.
However, pursuant to Article 2(1)(d) (ii) of MiFID II, when a person dealing on own account in financial instruments other than commodity derivatives or emission allowances or derivatives thereof and not providing any other investment services or performing any other investment activities in such instruments is also a member of or a participant in a regulated market or an MTF, it falls under the scope of MiFID II, and should accordingly be authorised as an investment firm unless:
it is exempted under points (a), (i) and (j); or
it is a non-financial entity which executes transactions on a trading venue which are objectively measurable as reducing risks directly relating to the commercial activity or treasury financing activity of that non-financial entity or its group.
As a consequence, the reference in Article 53(3) to persons other than investment firms and credit institutions only relates to entities that are exempted from authorisation under Article 2(1), such as insurance companies or collective investment undertakings, as long as their own regulatory framework permits them to do so.
This Q&A does not address the issue of non-EEA firms being a member or participant of an EEA trading venue.

meta.legal_act: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II) Directive 2014/65/EU- Secondary Markets
meta.subject_matter: Unauthorised person as an investment firm meeting the requirements of Article 53(3) of MiFID II being a member or participant of a regulated market or an MTF

baseline.text:
Under MiFID II, a person who is not authorised as an investment firm but satisfies the conditions set out in Article 53(3) of Directive 2014/65/EU is legally permitted to act as a member or participant of a regulated market or a Multilateral Trading Facility (MTF). Article 53(3) explicitly defines such an entity as an "unauthorised person" that meets specific criteria, including being a financial institution authorised in a third country or a financial market operator authorised in a third country, provided they comply with the relevant third-country regulatory regime. The Directive further clarifies that these unauthorised persons may participate in regulated markets or MTFs if they are members or participants, subject to the conditions laid down in Article 53(3) and the provisions of Article 53(4) regarding the supervision of their activities.

Crucially, the regulatory framework distinguishes between the status of the entity and its operational capacity within the EU market infrastructure. While the entity does not hold an EU investment firm authorisation, its participation in a regulated market or MTF does not automatically render it an investment firm under Article 4(1)(A) of the Directive, provided it strictly adheres to the exemptions and conditions outlined in Article 53. This distinction ensures that third-country entities can access EU trading venues without the full burden of EU authorisation, provided their home jurisdiction offers equivalent protection and regulatory oversight.

However, this permission is not absolute; it is contingent upon the entity fulfilling the specific requirements of Article 53(3), which include maintaining adequate capital, ensuring robust risk management, and complying with the laws of their home Member State or third country. Furthermore, if the unauthorised person engages in activities beyond those permitted under Article 53(3), such as providing investment services or advice to retail clients, they would fall under the definition of an investment firm and would require full authorisation under Article 4(1)(A). Therefore, the ability to participate in a regulated market or MTF is a specific privilege granted to unauthorised persons meeting Article 53(3) criteria, distinct from the general definition of an investment firm, and must be exercised in strict compliance with the supervisory expectations and reporting obligations detailed in the Directive.

dpo.text:
Under MiFID II, a person who is not authorised as an investment firm but satisfies the conditions set out in Article 53(3) of Directive 2014/65/EU is legally permitted to act as a member or participant of a regulated market or a Multilateral Trading Facility (MTF). Article 53(3) explicitly defines such an entity as an "unauthorised person" that meets specific criteria, including being a financial institution authorised in a third country or a financial market operator authorised in a third country, provided they comply with the relevant third-country regulations and are subject to supervision by a competent authority in that third country [Directive 2014/65/EU, Article 53(3)].

The regulatory framework distinguishes between authorised investment firms and these unauthorised persons regarding their capacity to participate in organised trading venues. While Article 2(1)(1) defines an investment firm as a person authorised under Article 4, Article 53(3) creates a distinct category allowing third-country entities to operate within the EU's organised markets without full EU authorisation, provided they adhere to the equivalence and supervision standards outlined in the Directive [Directive 2014/65/EU, Article 53(3)]. Consequently, the prohibition on unauthorised persons acting as investment firms does not extend to their status as market participants, as long as they fall within the narrow scope of Article 53(3).

This interpretation is reinforced by the EBA's technical standards and guidance, which clarify that the definition of a member or participant in a regulated market or MTF encompasses both authorised investment firms and unauthorised persons meeting Article 53(3) requirements [EBA/ESMA Guidelines on Market Participant Status]. Therefore, the mere lack of EU investment firm authorisation is not a disqualifying factor for market participation if the entity strictly complies with the third-country authorisation and supervision mandates established by Article 53(3). This ensures that third-country financial operators can access EU organised markets under a regime of equivalence, maintaining market integrity while facilitating cross-border financial services [Directive 2014/65/EU, Article 53(3)].

question: For application of the grandfathering rules defined in Article 484 CRR and following, does the change in debtor resulting from a merger means that a new capital instrument has been issued and that its eligibility for grandfathering or for full eligibility as an own fund instrument should be assessed at the date of the merger or should one use the initial characteristics of the bond?
ground_truth:
As specified in
Q&A 2013_16
, changes made to pre-CRR instruments shall aim at ensuring a full eligibility under the provisions of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 but shall not aim at allowing a grandfathering of the instrument. For the case at hand, a change of the debtor or the legal format shall not per se be regarded as a material change and does not necessarily lead to the requalification as a new instrument.
According to Article 484(2) CRR, the provisions of Article 484 CRR regarding the eligibility for grandfathering of own funds instruments apply to the instrument of Bank 2 from 1 January 2014, provided that the instrument qualified as own funds under the national transposition measures for Directive 2006/48/EC on 31 December 2011.
The prevailing swap rates and credit margins on the merger date are not relevant to assess the eligibility for grandfathering or the compliance with the CRR criteria on own funds instruments.

meta.subject_matter: Grandfathering of own funds instruments

baseline.text: Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the application of grandfathering rules regarding own funds instruments is strictly tied to the specific characteristics of the instrument at the time of its initial issuance, not subsequent corporate restructuring events such as mergers. Article 484(1) CRR establishes that instruments issued prior to the entry into force of the CRR may be grandfathered provided they meet specific criteria, including the requirement that the instrument was issued in accordance with the law of the Member State at the time of issuance [CRR, Article 484(1)]. The regulatory framework does not mandate a reassessment of eligibility based on the identity of the debtor following a merger. Instead, the eligibility determination relies on the substantive features of the bond as they existed when it was originally created. Consequently, if an instrument qualified for grandfathering based on its initial terms, the change in legal entity resulting from a merger does not retroactively invalidate that status nor does it trigger a requirement to re-evaluate the instrument against current standards as if it were a new issuance. The initial characteristics of the bond remain the definitive benchmark for assessing eligibility under the grandfathering regime. This approach ensures legal certainty and prevents the erosion of capital adequacy standards through post-issuance structural changes that do not alter the fundamental nature of the debt obligation. Therefore, regulators and supervisors must assess the instrument using the parameters established at the date of its original issuance, disregarding the subsequent change in debtor status arising from the merger. This interpretation aligns with the principle that grandfathering is a transitional measure intended to recognize existing capital structures without imposing the full burden of current technical standards on instruments that were compliant under the previous regulatory environment at the time of their launch.

dpo.text:
Under Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR), the application of grandfathering rules regarding own funds instruments is strictly tied to the specific characteristics of the instrument at the time of its original issuance, not subsequent corporate restructuring events. Article 484(1) CRR establishes that instruments issued prior to 1 January 2014 may be grandfathered provided they meet specific eligibility criteria, including those regarding the nature of the underlying assets and the seniority of the claim. The regulatory framework does not treat a change in the debtor resulting from a merger as a new issuance of capital. Consequently, the eligibility assessment must rely on the initial characteristics of the bond as they stood at the date of its original issuance [CRR, Article 484(1)].

The rationale underpinning this approach is that the risk profile and the fundamental nature of the instrument—such as its maturity, coupon structure, and subordination—remain unchanged by the identity of the issuing entity, provided the legal obligations are effectively transferred. A merger alters the legal personality of the issuer but does not alter the contractual terms of the debt instrument itself. Therefore, if an instrument was eligible for grandfathering based on its initial terms, it retains that status post-merger. Conversely, if the instrument failed to meet the grandfathering criteria at issuance, the merger does not retroactively validate its eligibility. The assessment date remains fixed at the issuance date to ensure consistency and prevent regulatory arbitrage through corporate restructurings [CRR, Article 484(1)].

Furthermore, the transitional provisions and the overarching principles of the Capital Requirements Regulation emphasize that grandfathering is a limited exception intended to address the specific regulatory environment of 2014, not a flexible mechanism adaptable to post-issuance structural changes. Any modification to the instrument's terms, such as a change in the debtor, would typically require a formal amendment to the contract. However, a mere change in the legal entity due to a merger, without a corresponding change in the bond's terms, does not constitute a new issuance. Thus, the initial characteristics of the bond are the sole determinant for its grandfathering status [CRR, Article 484(1)].

question:
We are seeking clarification about a possible mismatch between ITS and DPM 3.5 (ID v22748_u - T1 L 06.00, column c0020) as part of the compilation of the template FC.06 Template - “Risk Concentration - Exposure by counterparties" within the FiCod. supervisory reporting.
The Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2454 of 14 December 2022 states that, within the Template FC.06 - “Risk Concentration - Exposure by counterparties", the exposures must be reported for each individual legal entity belonging to the financial conglomerate, whereas the DPM 3.5 only permit reporting a unique value of the identification code of the external counterparty. This also determines the impossibility of representing separately the exposures held towards the same external counterparty but denominated in different currencies.
We therefore ask what is the correct way to represent - inside the FC.06 Template- the cases in which multiple entities belonging to the conglomerate have exposures towards the same external counterparty and for the cases in which, for each external counterparty, there are exposures denominated in different currencies.

The modelling (DPM) of template
L 06.00 - Risk Concentration - Exposure by counterparties

0090 - ID code of the entity of the financial conglomerate, 0030 - ID code type of the external counterparty and 0100 - ID code Type of the entity of the financial conglomerate

Identification code of the external counterparty
, ensuring the uniqueness of all rows to be reported in this open row template when several entities of the financial conglomerate have exposures with the same external counterparty.
As an interim solution, until the abovementioned amendment has been implemented in the modelling, in case more than one entity of the financial conglomerate has exposures with a specific external counterparty, report in column 0020 -
Identification code of the external counterparty
a merged version of the IDs in scope for 0020 -
Identification code of the external counterparty
and 0090 -
ID code of the entity of the financial conglomerate,
by that creating a unique value for all rows reported in this template.

Regarding column 0240 – Currency of template
L 06.00

meta.subject_matter: Financial Conglomerates: Mismatch between ITS and DPM 3.5 – ID v22748_u - T1 L 06.00, column c0020.

baseline.text:
The discrepancy identified between the Information Transmission System (ITS) and the Data Processing Manual (DPM) 3.5 regarding Template FC.06 stems from a fundamental difference in the reporting granularity mandated by the underlying legal framework versus the technical implementation constraints. Directive 2002/87/EC (FiCOD), specifically Article 10(1), requires financial conglomerates to report risk concentrations for each individual legal entity within the group. Consequently, the supervisory reporting template FC.06 is designed to capture exposures at the legal entity level to ensure granular oversight of intra-group and external exposures. However, the DPM 3.5, which governs the technical transmission of this data, specifies that the external counterparty identification code (ID) must be unique per row. This technical limitation does not preclude the reporting of multiple exposures; rather, it necessitates that each exposure line item be associated with the specific legal entity holding that exposure.

To resolve the issue of multiple exposures towards the same external counterparty, the reporting entity must submit a separate line item for each legal entity involved. If Entity A and Entity B both hold exposures to Counterparty X, two distinct rows must be generated in the FC.06 template. The first row will contain the identification code of Entity A and the corresponding exposure amount to Counterparty X, while the second row will contain the identification code of Entity B and the exposure amount to the same Counterparty X. This approach satisfies the Directive's requirement for entity-specific reporting while adhering to the DPM's constraint on the uniqueness of the counterparty ID within a single row.

Regarding exposures denominated in different currencies, the same logic applies. The template does not aggregate amounts by currency for a single legal entity and counterparty pair. Instead, each currency denomination must be reported in a separate line item. For a single legal entity holding exposures to the same external counterparty in EUR and USD, two rows are required. The first row reports the EUR amount with the appropriate currency code, and the second row reports the USD amount. This structure ensures that the supervisory authority receives a complete picture of the risk concentration, distinguishing clearly between the legal entity, the external counterparty, and the currency denomination, thereby aligning the technical submission with the substantive requirements of FiCOD.

dpo.text:
The discrepancy identified between the Information Transmission System (ITS) and the Data Processing Manual (DPM) 3.5 regarding Template FC.06 stems from a fundamental difference in the reporting granularity mandated by the underlying legal framework versus the technical implementation constraints. Directive 2002/87/EC (FiCOD), specifically Article 10(1), requires financial conglomerates to report risk concentrations for each individual legal entity within the group. Consequently, the template design necessitates that exposures be broken down by the specific legal entity holding the position. However, the DPM 3.5 specification for column c0020 allows for a single unique value for the external counterparty's identification code across all rows, which technically precludes the simultaneous reporting of multiple distinct exposures to the same counterparty in different currencies within a single submission instance.

To resolve this, the supervisory reporting framework mandates that the reporting entity must aggregate exposures by external counterparty only when the exposures are denominated in the same currency. For exposures held by different legal entities of the conglomerate towards the same external counterparty, the data must be reported separately for each legal entity, utilizing the same counterparty ID in column c0020 for all rows corresponding to that counterparty. This approach ensures compliance with the FiCOD requirement to report on a legal entity basis while adhering to the DPM's structural limitations.

Regarding exposures denominated in different currencies, the correct representation requires splitting the reporting lines. If a single legal entity holds exposures to the same external counterparty in multiple currencies, these must be reported as separate rows within the template. Each row must contain the specific currency denomination and the corresponding exposure amount, while the counterparty identification code in column c0020 remains identical for all rows pertaining to that specific external counterparty. This method allows the supervisor to distinguish between currency-specific risk concentrations without violating the technical constraint of reporting a unique counterparty ID per row. This interpretation aligns with the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2454, which clarifies that the template serves to capture risk concentration data at the level of the legal entity, necessitating a row-level aggregation strategy for multi-currency scenarios.

question: Is the exemption of applying strong customer authentication, in respect of legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions through the use of dedicated payment processes or protocols that are only made available to payers who are not consumers applicable to both payment initiation and account information services? Or, is it solely applicable to payment initiation service?
ground_truth:
Article 17 of the
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389
states that payment service providers may decide not to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) “in respect of legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions through the use of dedicated payment processes or protocols that are only made available to payers who are not consumers”, provided competent authorities are satisfied that the levels of security are equivalent to those provided for by Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2). This exemption applies solely to payment initiation, given it refers to “legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions”; it does not apply to account information.
Payment initiation as a process is not to be confused with payment initiation services, with the latter referring to a payment that is initiated by a third party.

meta.topic: Strong customer authentication and common and secure communication (incl. access)
meta.subject_matter: Exemption of secure corporate payment processes and protocols

baseline.text:
Under Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2), the exemption from the requirement to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) for legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions via dedicated payment processes or protocols is applicable to both the payment initiation service (PIS) and the account information service (AIS). This exemption is explicitly granted in Article 30(1)(a) of the Directive, which states that the SCA requirement does not apply to a legal person initiating a payment transaction through a dedicated payment process or protocol that is only made available to payers who are not consumers. The legislative intent behind this provision is to facilitate efficient corporate payment flows while maintaining security for non-consumer entities.

Crucially, the scope of this exemption extends beyond PIS to encompass AIS. While Article 30(1)(a) is situated within the section governing PIS, the regulatory framework and subsequent EBA/ESMA guidance clarify that the underlying principle of exempting SCA for dedicated corporate protocols applies uniformly across the relevant services where such protocols are utilized. The exemption is not limited to the act of initiating a payment but covers the broader ecosystem of secure communication and access for legal persons. Consequently, when a legal person utilizes a dedicated protocol available exclusively to non-consumer payers to access account information or initiate payments, the SCA requirement is waived for both activities. This ensures that corporate entities can operate seamlessly without the administrative burden of SCA, provided the protocol remains restricted to non-consumer users. The exemption is therefore not solely applicable to PIS but is a cross-cutting measure for dedicated corporate protocols within both PIS and AIS.

dpo.text: Under Directive 2015/2366/EU (PSD2), the exemption from the requirement to apply strong customer authentication (SCA) for legal persons initiating electronic payment transactions via dedicated payment processes or protocols is applicable to both the payment initiation service (PIS) and the account information service (AIS). This exemption is explicitly granted in Article 30(1)(a) of the Directive, which states that the SCA requirement does not apply to a legal person initiating a payment transaction through a dedicated payment process or protocol that is only made available to payers who are not consumers. While the primary operational focus of such dedicated protocols is often the execution of payments under PIS, the legislative text does not restrict this exemption to PIS alone. Consequently, when a legal person utilizes a dedicated protocol to access account information for non-consumer payers, the SCA requirement is similarly waived under the same provision. The European Banking Authority and European Securities and Markets Authority have consistently interpreted this clause to cover any service where the dedicated protocol is exclusively accessible to non-consumer legal entities, ensuring that the streamlined authentication framework applies uniformly across both service types provided the access restriction criteria are met. This interpretation aligns with the Directive's objective of facilitating efficient corporate payment flows while maintaining security standards for consumer-facing services. Therefore, the exemption is not limited to payment initiation but extends to account information services when the specific conditions regarding the payer's status and the exclusivity of the protocol are satisfied.

question: Paragraphs 40) and 41) of the Guidelines on performance fees recommend that the length of the performance reference period  (if this is shorter than the whole life of the fund) should be set equal to at least 5 years. How should the performance reference period be set for the first time in light of the application date of the guidelines?
ground_truth:
[ESMA 34-43-392 UCITS Q&A, Section 11, 2a] & [ESMA 34-32-352 AIFMD Q&A, Section 15, 2]
Managers of any funds already compliant with paragraphs 40)
[1]
and 41)
[2]
of the Guidelines on performance fees before the application date of the guidelines should look at the past 5 years/whole life of the fund for the purpose of setting the performance reference period
[3]
(i.e. they should not reset the performance reference period after the application date of the guidelines).
In all the other cases, managers should apply the performance reference period starting from the beginning of the financial year following 6 months from the application date of the Guidelines (i.e. the performance reference period should start at the beginning of the financial year following 5 July 2021; by way of example, if the financial year of the fund starts on 1 September 2021, the period 1 September 2021 – 1 September 2022 should be considered as the first year of the performance reference period).
[1]
Paragraph 40) of the Guidelines on performance fees states that “In case the fund employs a performance fee model based on a benchmark index, it should be ensured that any underperformance of the fund compared to the benchmark is clawed back before any performance fee becomes payable. To this purpose, the length of the performance reference period, if this is shorter than the whole life of the fund, should be set equal to at least 5 years.”
[2]
Paragraph 41) of the Guidelines on performance fees states that “Where a fund utilises a HWM model, a performance fee should be payable only where, during the performance reference period, the new HWM exceeds the last HWM. The starting point to be considered in the calculations should be the initial offering price per share. For the HWM model, in case the performance reference period is shorter than the whole life of the fund, the performance reference period should be set equal to at least five years on a rolling basis. In this case, performance fee may only be claimed if the outperformance exceeds any underperformances during the previous five years and performance fees should not crystallise more than once a year”.
[3]
This is defined as “the time horizon over which the performance is measured and compared with that of the reference indicator, at the end of which the mechanism for the compensation for past underperformance (or negative performance) can be reset”.

meta.legal_act: Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities Directive (UCITS) Directive 2009/65/EC
meta.subject_matter: Timeline of the application of the performance reference period

baseline.text: The application of the Guidelines on performance fees, adopted under Article 10(1) of Directive 2009/65/EC, is governed by a specific transitional timeline established in Article 10(2) of the Directive itself. While the Guidelines recommend that the performance reference period be set at a minimum of five years to ensure sufficient data for meaningful risk assessment, the timing of this recommendation's application depends on the fund's status at the moment the Guidelines enter into force. For funds that are already in operation when the Guidelines become applicable, the recommendation regarding the five-year minimum period applies immediately to any new performance fee arrangements entered into thereafter. This is because the Guidelines do not mandate a retroactive adjustment of existing contractual terms but rather set standards for future conduct. Consequently, a fund manager must assess the current date against the entry-into-force date of the Guidelines. If the Guidelines were adopted on 10 December 2014, as per the Official Journal of the European Union, then for any new performance fee agreement concluded on or after that date, the reference period must be at least five years. However, for funds established prior to this date, the obligation to adhere to the five-year minimum only triggers upon the conclusion of a new performance fee arrangement post-implementation. The Guidelines explicitly state that they apply to all UCITS funds, but the practical implementation relies on the distinction between existing and new contractual engagements. Therefore, the timeline dictates that the five-year minimum is a forward-looking requirement for new agreements, ensuring that the performance reference period aligns with the regulatory intent to prevent short-termism, without imposing immediate structural changes on legacy funds unless they enter into new fee arrangements. [Directive 2009/65/EC, Article 10(2)]

dpo.text: The application of the Guidelines on performance fees, adopted under Article 10(2) of Directive 2009/65/EC, is governed by the transitional provisions set out in Article 10(3) of the Directive itself. While the Guidelines recommend that the performance reference period be at least five years to ensure a sufficient historical basis for assessing manager performance, the timing of this requirement is strictly contingent upon the date the Guidelines enter into force. According to the EBA's analysis of the legal framework, the Guidelines were adopted on 18 December 2014 and entered into force on 19 January 2015. Consequently, the recommendation regarding the five-year minimum period applies only to funds established or modified on or after this entry-into-force date. For funds existing prior to 19 January 2015, the requirement to adopt a five-year performance reference period does not automatically apply retroactively. Instead, such funds must adhere to the performance fee structures and reference periods that were in force at the time of their initial establishment or last significant modification, provided such structures complied with the relevant provisions of the UCITS Directive and its implementing measures as they stood at that time. The EBA has clarified that national competent authorities should not impose the new five-year standard on legacy funds unless a specific national transposition measure or subsequent amendment to the Directive mandates such a change. Therefore, the timeline for applying the five-year rule begins exclusively from the date the Guidelines became legally binding, ensuring a harmonized approach across the EU while respecting the legal certainty afforded to existing fund structures. This interpretation aligns with the principle of legal certainty enshrined in EU law, preventing retroactive disruption to established investment vehicles.

In such case, would any general prior permission to repurchase CET 1 instruments for discretionary trading activity over treasury shares purposes result in a deduction from own funds at the time when the permission is granted or would a deduction from own funds be made at the time when the relevant repurchase of CET 1 instruments takes place?
ground_truth:
